[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Texas_population_pyramid.webp/250px-Texas_population_pyramid.webp.png)](/wiki/File:Texas_population_pyramid.webp)

Texas [population pyramid](/wiki/Population_pyramid "Population pyramid")

According to the [U.S. Census Bureau](/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), as of 2023, [Texas](/wiki/Texas "Texas") was the [second largest state in population](/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_by_population "List of U.S. states by population") after [California](/wiki/California "California"), with a population of 30,503,301, an increase of more than 1.3 million people, or 4.7%, since the 29,145,505 of the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").[[1]](#cite_note-:1-1)[[2]](#cite_note-:5-2) Its apportioned population in 2020 was 29,183,290.[[3]](#cite_note-:6-3) Since the beginning of the 21st century, the state of Texas has experienced strong population growth.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) Texas has many major cities and metropolitan areas, along with many towns and rural areas. Much of the population is concentrated in the major cities of [Dallas–Fort Worth](/wiki/Dallas%E2%80%93Fort_Worth_metroplex "Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex"), [Austin](/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"), [San Antonio](/wiki/San_Antonio "San Antonio"), [Houston](/wiki/Houston "Houston"), [McAllen](/wiki/McAllen,_Texas "McAllen, Texas"), [Brownsville](/wiki/Brownsville,_Texas "Brownsville, Texas"), [El Paso](/wiki/El_Paso,_Texas "El Paso, Texas"), and their corresponding [metropolitan areas](/wiki/List_of_Texas_metropolitan_areas "List of Texas metropolitan areas"). The first four aforementioned main urban centers are also referred to as the [Texas Triangle megaregion](/wiki/Texas_Triangle "Texas Triangle").

[Nationwide protests](/wiki/2022_COVID-19_protests_in_China "2022 COVID-19 protests in China") broke out in November 2022 amid growing discontent among residents over the zero-COVID policy and the resulting economic costs.[[53]](#cite_note-china_protests-53) Following the easing of the Zero-COVID strategy in December 2022, Beijing reported a surge in COVID-19 infections.[[54]](#cite_note-54)[[55]](#cite_note-55) It was reported that restaurants and food delivery services had closed due to staff infections, and pharmacies had been emptied of medicine and disinfectant solution.[[56]](#cite_note-56) On 22 December, a report by UK research firm Airfinity modelling based on regional Chinese data estimated that more than 5,000 people were dying each day from COVID-19 in China, with cases rising fastest in Beijing and Guangdong province.[[57]](#cite_note-57) Internal minutes from a meeting of China's National Health Commission held on 21 December revealed that as many as 248 million people in China might have contracted COVID-19 over the first 20 days of December, and up to 37 million on a single day.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

On 23 December 2022 [Qingdao](/wiki/Qingdao "Qingdao")'s municipal health chief Bo Tao stated that the city was seeing "between 490,000 and 530,000" new infections each day and on the same day, [Dongguan](/wiki/Dongguan "Dongguan")'s health commission declared on its Weixin account that the city had 250,000 to 300,000 people being infected every day.[[59]](#cite_note-59) Officials in [Yulin](/wiki/Yulin,_Shaanxi "Yulin, Shaanxi"), a city of 3.6 million people in Shaanxi province, logged 157,000 new infections with models estimating more than a third of the city's population had already been infected.[[60]](#cite_note-60) On 25 December 2022, the National Health Commission announced that it would no longer report daily COVID-19 figures,[[61]](#cite_note-61) and Zhejiang prov

In July 1776, the [Thirteen Colonies](/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies"), represented at the [Second Continental Congress](/wiki/Second_Continental_Congress "Second Continental Congress") in [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), unanimously adopted the [United States Declaration of Independence](/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence") in which the colonies declared themselves to be independent [sovereign states](/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") and no longer under [British](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") rule.[[22]](#cite_note-Milkis-26) The affirmation was made in the [Declaration of Independence](/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence"), which was written predominantly by [Thomas Jefferson](/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") and adopted unanimously on July 4, 1776, by the Second Continental Congress. Recognizing the necessity of closely coordinating their efforts against the [British](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain"),[[23]](#cite_note-Kelly-27) the Continental Congress simultaneously began the process of drafting a constitution that would bind the [states](/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") together. There were long debates on a number of issues, including representation and voting, and the exact powers to be given the central government.[[24]](#cite_note-28) Congress finished work on the [Articles of Confederation](/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") to establish a [perpetual union](/wiki/Perpetual_Union "Perpetual Union") between the states in November 1777 and sent it to the states for [ratification](/wiki/Ratification "Ratification").[[22]](#cite_note-Milkis-26)

fanoutqa_026622.x:
Cuban Missile Crisis :: Background :: Cuba–Soviet relations :: chunk_0005
Main article: [Escalante affair](/wiki/Escalante_affair "Escalante affair")

In late 1961, [Fidel Castro](/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro") asked for more SA-2 anti-aircraft missiles from the [Soviet Union](/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). The request was not acted upon by the Soviet leadership. In the interval, Castro began criticizing the Soviets for lack of "revolutionary boldness", and began talking to [China](/wiki/China "China") about agreements for economic assistance. In March 1962, Castro ordered the ousting of [Anibal Escalante](/wiki/Anibal_Escalante "Anibal Escalante") and his pro-Moscow comrades from Cuba's [Integrated Revolutionary Organizations](/wiki/Integrated_Revolutionary_Organizations "Integrated Revolutionary Organizations"). This affair alarmed the Soviet leadership and raised fears of a possible US invasion. As a result, the Soviet Union sent more SA-2 anti-aircraft missiles in April, as well as a regiment of regular Soviet troops.[[7]](#cite_note-Kennedy-7)

Historian [Timothy Naftali](/wiki/Timothy_Naftali "Timothy Naftali") writes that Escalante's dismissal was a motivating factor behind the Soviet decision to place nuclear missiles in Cuba in 1962. According to Naftali, Soviet foreign policy planners were concerned that Castro's break with Escalante foreshadowed a Cuban drift toward [China](/wiki/China "China"), and they sought to solidify the Soviet-Cuban relationship through the missile basing program.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Sketch of a regular icosahedron by Johannes Kepler

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Mysterium_Cosmographicum_solar_system_model.jpg/250px-Mysterium_Cosmographicum_solar_system_model.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mysterium_Cosmographicum_solar_system_model.jpg)

[Kepler's](/wiki/Johannes_Kepler "Johannes Kepler") Platonic solid model of the [Solar System](/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System")

The regular icosahedron is one of the five [Platonic solids](/wiki/Platonic_solid "Platonic solid"). The regular polyhedra have been known since antiquity, but are named after [Plato](/wiki/Plato "Plato") who, in his [*Timaeus*](/wiki/Timaeus_(dialogue) "Timaeus (dialogue)") dialogue, identified these with the five [elements](/wiki/Classical_elements "Classical elements"), whose elementary units were attributed these shapes: [fire](/wiki/Fire_(classical_element) "Fire (classical element)") (tetrahedron), [air](/wiki/Air_(classical_element) "Air (classical element)") (octahedron), [water](/wiki/Water_(classical_element) "Water (classical element)") (icosahedron), [earth](/wiki/Earth_(classical_element) "Earth (classical element)") (cube) and the shape of the universe as a whole (dodecahedron). [Euclid](/wiki/Euclid "Euclid")'s [*Elements*](/wiki/Euclid%27s_Elements "Euclid's Elements") defined the Platonic solids and solved the problem of finding the ratio of the circumscribed sphere's diameter to the edge length.[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeath1908262,_478,_480-40)

Following their identification with the elements by Plato, [Johannes Kepler](/wiki/Johannes_Kepler "Johannes Kepler") in his *[Harmonices Mundi](/wiki/Harmonices_Mundi "Harmonices Mundi")* sketched each of them, in particular, the regular icosahedron.[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECromw

fanoutqa_012286.x:
Ryan Fitzpatrick :: Professional career :: Buffalo Bills :: 2011 season :: chunk_0007
During a Week 2 comeback 38–35 victory over the [Oakland Raiders](/wiki/2011_Oakland_Raiders_season "2011 Oakland Raiders season"), Fitzpatrick led the Bills to touchdown drives on five straight possessions in the second half.[[42]](#cite_note-42) It was the first time in league history a team had scored offensive touchdowns on five straight possessions in the second half.[[43]](#cite_note-43) He was named the AFC Offensive Player of the Month for September.

On October 28, 2011, Fitzpatrick signed a six-year, $59 million contract extension including a $10 million signing bonus with the Bills.[[44]](#cite_note-44) He had three 300-yard performances in the 2011 season, with a season-high 369 yards during a Week 3 34–31 comeback victory over the [New England Patriots](/wiki/2011_New_England_Patriots_season "2011 New England Patriots season").[[45]](#cite_note-45)

After the 2011 season, it was revealed that Fitzpatrick had broken his ribs in a game against the [Washington Redskins](/wiki/2011_Washington_Redskins_season "2011 Washington Redskins season"), which was presumably a factor in his decline in play over the rest of the season. Fitzpatrick finished the 2011 season with 3,832 passing yards, 24 touchdowns, and a league-leading 23 interceptions to go along with 56 carries for 215 yards in 16 games and starts.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

Netflix did not initially reveal subscriber viewership numbers for their original series, and [Symphony Technology Group](/wiki/Symphony_Technology_Group "Symphony Technology Group") compiled data for the season based on people using software on their phones that measures television viewing by detecting a program's sound. According to Symphony, within the first 35 days of release, *Stranger Things* averaged ratings of around 14.07 million adults between the ages of 18 and 49 in the United States. This made it the third most-watched season of Netflix original content in the [U.S](/wiki/United_States "United States"). at the time behind the first season of *[Fuller House](/wiki/Fuller_House_(TV_series) "Fuller House (TV series)")* and [fourth season](/wiki/Orange_Is_the_New_Black_season_4 "Orange Is the New Black season 4") of *[Orange Is the New Black](/wiki/Orange_Is_the_New_Black "Orange Is the New Black")*.[[109]](#cite_note-111) In a September 2016 analysis, Netflix found that *Stranger Things* "hooked" viewers by the second episode of the first season, indicating that the second episode was "the first installment that led at least 70 percent of viewers who watched that episode to complete the entire first season of the show".[[110]](#cite_note-112)

For the third season, Netflix revealed that the show had broken viewing records for Netflix, with 40.7 million households having watched the show in its first four days, and 18.2 million already watched the entire series within that time frame.[[111]](#cite_note-113) Within its first month, the third season was watched by 64 million households, setting a new record for the most-watched original Netflix series.[[112]](#cite_note-114)[[113]](#cite_note-115)

The series is the most followed TV show on social media app *[TV Time](/wiki/TV_Time "TV Time")*'s history, with over 5 million followers.[[114]](#cite_note-TV_Time_2016-116)

Mars :: part 03 :: chunk_0002
**Mars** is the fourth [planet](/wiki/Planet "Planet") from the [Sun](/wiki/Sun "Sun"). It is also known as the "**Red Planet**", for [its orange-red](/wiki/Mars_surface_color "Mars surface color") appearance.[[22]](#cite_note-Rees2012-24)[[23]](#cite_note-nasa_hematite-25) Mars is a desert-like [rocky planet](/wiki/Rocky_planet "Rocky planet") with a tenuous [atmosphere](/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Mars "Atmosphere of Mars") that is primarily [carbon dioxide](/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") (CO2). At the average surface level the atmospheric pressure is a few thousandths of [Earth](/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s, atmospheric temperature ranges from −153 to 20 °C (−243 to 68 °F),[[24]](#cite_note-p167-26) and [cosmic radiation](/wiki/Cosmic_radiation "Cosmic radiation") is high. Mars retains some water, [in the ground](/wiki/Groundwater_on_Mars "Groundwater on Mars") as well as thinly in the atmosphere, forming [cirrus clouds](/wiki/Cirrus_cloud "Cirrus cloud"), [fog](/wiki/Fog "Fog"), [frost](/wiki/Frost "Frost"), larger polar regions of [permafrost](/wiki/Permafrost "Permafrost") and [ice caps](/wiki/Martian_polar_ice_caps "Martian polar ice caps") (with seasonal CO2 snow), but no bodies of liquid surface water. Its surface gravity is roughly a third of Earth's or double that of the Moon. Its diameter, 6,779 km (4,212 mi), is about [half the Earth](/wiki/List_of_Solar_System_objects_by_size "List of Solar System objects by size")'s, or twice the Moon's, and its surface area is the size of all the dry land of Earth.[[25]](#cite_note-27)
